html:
The Hippocratic Oath is a Greek oath of ethics for doctors, probably written in the late 5th or 4th century BCE. It comes down to us among the writings of the school of Hippocrates on the island of Kos, though he may not have written it himself.

The new doctor swears by Apollo, the healing god Asclepius, whose great sanctuary was at Epidaurus, and the goddesses of health. He promises:

  • to treat his teacher like a parent and teach the art to the teacher's sons without fee
  • to use treatment to help the sick and never to harm or wrong them
  • not to give a deadly drug, even if asked, and not to give a woman a pessary to cause abortion
  • to keep secret what he sees and hears in patients' homes

The famous phrase "first, do no harm" is not in it, though the idea is. It is the earliest statement of medical ethics in the West. Many medical schools still have students swear a modern version, such as the World Medical Association's Declaration of Geneva of 1948.
